title: A Comprehensive View of Fairness through Distributional Stability
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Our stability-based method traces a better accuracy-fairness frontier than constrained, post-processing and robust baselines across datasets and fairness notions.
layout: 2x4 grid of line plots, shared legend on top, columns by dataset/metric
description: A grid of eight scatter-line plots in two rows and four columns, with one shared legend on top. The legend lists STABLE (blue), ERM + constraint (orange), PostProc (green), STABLE_DRO (brown), and a red star for ERM. Columns are labeled (a) Adult DP, (b) Adult EO, (c) COMPAS DP, (d) COMPAS EO. The top row plots accuracy against unfairness U(h). The bottom row plots accuracy against deployment gap. Each curve is a sequence of dots tracing a frontier, with translucent shaded bands showing standard deviation along the horizontal axis. Arrows mark that higher accuracy and lower unfairness or gap are better. The blue STABLE curve usually sits toward the upper left, especially in the deployment-gap row. The eye goes first to the blue curves and the red ERM star near the top.
caption: Accuracy–unfairness (top) and accuracy–deployment-gap (bottom) frontiers on Adult and COMPAS. Each point corresponds to one fairness budget of the common grid, averaged over 10 seeds; shaded regions show ± one standard deviation along the horizontal axis.
abstract: We view fairness as a property of distributional stability. Rather than assessing a predictor under a fixed data distribution, we study how its predictions change under perturbations that modify the composition of protected groups. A predictor is fair if it remains stable under such shifts. Under this perspective, several classical notions of fairness arise as stability with respect to specific perturbations, with the associated unfairness gap given by a Lipschitz constant of a prediction-rate functional. This formulation also yields guarantees that hold uniformly over a range of demographic compositions at test time, without requiring knowledge of the deployment distribution. It leads to a learning procedure based on convex combinations of reweighted predictors, formulated as a second-order cone program, for which we establish generalization bounds. Experiments on standard benchmarks illustrate the approach.
